title: Lane negotiation and fractional hold PRD notes
body:
Summary:

This doc captures an early PRD sketch for Lane Negotiation + Fractional Hold: a lightweight commitment model that lets customers acquire small, short-lived capacity guarantees (fractional GPU-seconds / lane credits) with automatic negotiation and graceful degradation semantics. The goal is to smooth microbursts for latency-sensitive workloads without forcing full reserved capacity or heavy-handed eviction.

High-level idea (one-liner):
- Allow customers to declare short-duration 'lane reservations' (e.g., N ms to M minutes) expressed in fractional capacity units. The system negotiates these lanes at admission time, either accepting, soft-accepting (best effort), or offering degraded fidelity/latency options.

Why (problem statement):
- Customers hate noisy neighbor latency spikes during short microbursts but often cannot justify full Dedicated capacity.
- Pure on-demand risks unpredictable tail latency for SLO-bound routes.
- Existing burst-credit models are coarse; fractional holds aim to provide fine-grained hedges and a negotiated degradation path that preserves critical requests.

Key concepts and terminology (stay small and pragmatic):
- Lane: a named QoS class with a latency and throughput band (e.g., hot, warm, cold).
- Fractional hold: a budgeted reservation token measured in fractional GPU-seconds or scaled-QLA units that can be consumed for prioritized scheduling over a short window.
- Timelock: holdback window; the fractional hold can include a minimum duration guarantee (timelock) after which it expires automatically.
- Soft-accept: lane accepted but marked as preemptible; system will attempt to satisfy but may degrade.
- Fidelity hint: API-level hint that indicates how much model fidelity to drop under degradation (temperature / lower-precision fallback / shorter generation).

Admission / Negotiation flow (API and runtime):
- Customer requests: route -> request options {lane_hint, min_hold, max_hold, fidelity_hint, priority_tag}
- Admission controller consults: current pool occupancy, active fractional holds, per-tenant SLO fingerprint, and configured lane quotas.
- Controller returns: {status: accept | soft_accept | offer_alternate_lane | reject, allocated_fraction, estimated_latency_range, charge_estimate}
- If offer_alternate_lane, client may accept or fallback to hosted fallback (if configured).

Billing & economics model (rough):
- Fractional holds billed at fine granularity (per-second-metered fractional units) with a small premium vs on-demand to reflect reservation value.
- Soft-accept discounts reflect preemptibility (e.g., 20–40% discount).
- Excess consumption beyond allocated_fraction is billed at higher on-demand rate or throttled depending on tenant policy.

Isolation and safety controls:
- Per-lane global caps and per-tenant rate windows to prevent a single tenant from starving lanes.
- Timelock expirations enforced by scheduler (hard reclaim after N seconds).
- Eviction ladder: fidelity downgrade -> rate limiting -> preemption. Preemption should be opt-in for tenants (policy flag).
- Audit logs for all lane negotiations with trace IDs for post-mortem.

Routing & fallback policies:
- Prefer local pool capacity for hot lanes; if unavailable, negotiate with cross-pool broker to borrow fractional credits (with cross-tenant safety gates).
- Multi-model fallback path: if the requested model is unavailable at the negotiated fidelity, automatically suggest a comparable model variant and include expected impact metrics in the response.

Operational metrics to track (simulator/telemetry):
- Admission acceptance rate per lane and per-tenant (target 95% for hot lanes).
- Fractional hold utilization (allocated vs consumed).
- Timelock reclaim latency (time between expiry and reclaim).
- Tail latency improvement for lanes vs control group.
- Number of alternate-lane offers issued and acceptance rate.

Console and UX sketch (product ask):
- Route-level toggle: enable lane negotiation.
- Slider for default fractional hold size and acceptable degradation (fidelity hint).
- Timeline view: active fractional holds with predicted expiry and consumption burn rate.
- Billing preview for a negotiation offer.

Runbook sketches (ops playbook):
- If hot lane acceptance rate < 80% for > 10m: run capacity-signal playbook: notify SRE + trigger predictive warm pool (link to playbook: CONFLUENCE-4821).
- If timelock reclaim latency spikes: inspect reclaim queue; escalate to infra autoscaler team (JIRA-DED-998).
- If cross-pool borrow failures exceed threshold: temporarily disable cross-borrow and surface to Console with recommended mitigation steps.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (labs): admission controller prototype + simulator (existing repo: dedicated-sim PR#27). Quick A/B tests with synthetic microbursts.
- Phase 1 (alpha): API+admission controller + sched reclaim + basic billing hooks. Limited tenants (internal + two partners).
- Phase 2 (beta): Console UX, cross-pool borrow, fidelity hint plumbing. Expand to more customers.
- Phase 3 (GA): SLAs, full billing integration, SLO-driven autoscale tie-ins.

Open questions / risks (short list):
- How to map fractional GPU-seconds to heterogeneous hardware (A100 vs H100 vs on-prem GPUs)? Need a normalized capacity unit (QLA) — propose a small working group with infra and research.
- Economic model complexity: fractional billing vs existing reserved billing may confuse customers. Need clear pricing tiers and a billing preview in UI.
- Edge cases with stateful model caches and KV eviction when preempting fractional holds.
- Incentives: customers may game short timelock churn; we need anti-abuse heuristics.

Short-term experiments (next 6 weeks):
- Run simulator sweep: sweep fractional hold sizes [0.1s, 0.5s, 1s, 5s per request-equivalent] against bursty traces from 5 customers (from telemetry) and measure tail latency reduction and cost overhead.
- Pilot with 2 internal teams: web search paraphrase service + autocomplete (low-fidelity degradation acceptable).
- Prototype console mock in Figma and run 3 user interviews with solutions engineers.

Work items (rough backlog):
- Spec API surface + request/response schema (owner: Riley)
- Admission controller proto + simulator integration (owner: Diego)
notes: doc is intentionally informal; intended to seed further product/eng discussion. Leave comments inline in Google Drive; link back to Confluence and JIRA for deeper specs.
